what_it_does: A MAC (multiply-accumulate) unit is the core building block of AI accelerators—it multiplies a number by a weight and adds it to a running total. If many operands are zero, you can skip those multiplications to save energy and time. This is called bit-level sparsity because zeros appear scattered throughout the bit patterns of numbers. FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays—chips you can reprogram in the field) are widely used for acceleration, but they struggle to exploit bit-level sparsity because their basic building blocks (LUTs, which are like tiny programmable logic gates) are poorly suited to the required computations. This paper presents an FPGA-friendly solution using adaptive encoding that maps efficiently to LUTs, combined with hardware that handles variable-latency operations (operations that take different amounts of time depending on how many zeros they encounter).
